section_summary: This section traces efforts to sell Japanese raw silk and fabrics after the war, including disputes over testing, tariffs, auction methods, export quotas, prices, and payment terms. Correspondence with British, Swiss, Indian, and other representatives addresses access to silk and the division of grades and deniers. Later documents discuss silk stocks and demand in 1948, followed by a Paterson industry complaint about Japanese fabric imports and a State Department response.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on silk exports, tariffs, and testing
subfiles.about: Magagna urges broader silk exports, tariff clarification, direct market sampling, and changes to U.S. Commercial Company practices.
subfiles.summary: The concluding pages argue that lower grade and higher denier silk could find U.S. buyers and earn dollars for Japan. Magagna recommends prompt tariff consultations and challenges reliance on the U.S. Testing Company for market advice.

subfiles.title: Draft message criticizing U.S. silk testing
subfiles.about: SCAP proposes bypassing the U.S. Testing Company bottleneck and consulting silk trade associations directly.
subfiles.summary: Draft message urges direct consultation with silk industry associations and criticizes reliance on a commercial tester.

subfiles.title: Draft message on Japanese silk testing and auction sales
subfiles.about: SCAP describes Japanese testing capacity and proposes sales using Japanese certificates and open auctions.
subfiles.summary: A revised draft reports testing capacity at Kobe and Yokohama, argues Japanese certificates can replace routine U.S. retesting, and repeats a proposal for Commodity Exchange auctions instead of sealed bids.

subfiles.title: Payment for Export Commodities in Kind
subfiles.to: Chief, Economic and Scientific Section, GHQ, SCAP
subfiles.about: Magagna proposes paying Japanese silk producers partly with food and equipment to revive production.
subfiles.summary: Magagna says inadequate payment is undermining cocoon farming and silk output. He proposes bartering surplus food and mechanical equipment to producers while criticizing export administration and uncompensated seizures.

subfiles.title: Duty on Textile Cloths
subfiles.about: SCAP requests urgent clarification of U.S. duties on silk and mixed textile cloth.
subfiles.summary: Draft requests a prompt customs ruling because textile duties affect Japan's export program.

subfiles.title: Textile Division administrative order
subfiles.from: W. F. Marquat, Chief, Economic and Scientific Section
subfiles.about: The order creates a Textile Division and defines its production, distribution, and export responsibilities.
subfiles.summary: Creates the Textile Division and assigns oversight of textile production, supplies, controls, and export coordination.

subfiles.title: Message requesting silk samples for U.S. trade groups
subfiles.about: SCAP requests samples of all silk types and grades for potential U.S. users.
subfiles.summary: Requests silk samples for New York trade groups and potential buyers.

subfiles.title: Message requesting samples for overseas markets
subfiles.about: SCAP proposes sending silk samples to Latin American and European markets, especially 42 denier silk.
subfiles.summary: Calls for overseas sampling of all grades, highlighting large Japanese stocks of 42 denier silk.

subfiles.title: Notes for message on raw silk testing
subfiles.about: Draft notes argue that Japanese testing certificates should support New York silk sales.
subfiles.summary: Notes compare Japanese testing capacity with delays and costs of U.S. retesting.

subfiles.title: Magagna cablegram to Congressman Flood
subfiles.about: Magagna urges action against sealed bid silk sales and demands market sampling of 42 denier silk.
subfiles.summary: Magagna asks Flood to intervene in silk sales policy and the makeup of the American Far Eastern Commission delegation.

subfiles.title: Raw Silk Testing
subfiles.about: SCAP recommends selling silk against Japanese tests and considering open auction sales.
subfiles.summary: The message reports expanded Japanese testing at Kobe and Yokohama and says reliance on Japanese certificates would remove a U.S. retesting bottleneck. It cites an offer by the New York Commodity Exchange to sell silk at open auction.

subfiles.title: British inquiry about Japanese silk exports
subfiles.about: Britain asks what quantities of silk are available and where exports will go.
subfiles.summary: McDougall asks about planned silk cloth shipments and British access to thrown silk.

subfiles.title: Reply on silk fabric availability
subfiles.about: Whitman reports silk fabric export targets and explains how Britain might arrange purchases.
subfiles.summary: Reports five million yards of habutae available and suggests British liaison with SCAP.

subfiles.title: Reply concerning Swiss-owned silk in Japan
subfiles.about: Martin explains why Swiss-owned silk cannot yet be released from blocked property.
subfiles.summary: Release of the prewar purchase requires an Inter-Allied policy agreement.

subfiles.title: Swiss request to export prewar silk purchase
subfiles.about: The Swiss legation seeks permission to export 38 bales bought before the Pacific war.
subfiles.summary: Schneeberger argues that the silk is Swiss property, already paid for and deteriorating in Yokohama storage. He requests advice on export permission.

subfiles.title: Invitation to meeting on raw silk quotas
subfiles.about: Whitman sets out questions for a September 9 meeting of interested governments.
subfiles.summary: Agenda covers grade allocations, exchanges between countries, New Zealand's quota, and pricing against U.S. sales.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram concerning investigation of Magagna
subfiles.about: The telegram reports a confidential SCAP investigation of Magagna's accusations.
subfiles.summary: Investigators confronted Magagna with earlier conversation memoranda that appeared inconsistent with his account of when he began opposing U.S. Commercial Company policy. Magagna disputed the memoranda and requested copies for Congressman Flood.

subfiles.title: Letter on prices for quota silk
subfiles.about: Whitman states the U.S. price basis for silk sold under Inter-Allied quotas.
subfiles.summary: Sealed bid prices should use a weighted average for the same type and grade.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation on silk quotas
subfiles.about: Representatives discuss allocations of scarce high grade silk among India, Australia, New Zealand, France, and Britain.
subfiles.summary: A U.S. Commercial Company table illustrates possible grade allocations. Participants raise no objection to India's proposed 15,000 bales of grade C and lower silk, but British and French representatives question high grade allocations for Australia and New Zealand. Whitman proposes limited allocations and possible Trade Board review.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of silk quota minutes to McDougall
subfiles.about: Whitman sends the September 23 silk quota meeting memorandum.
subfiles.summary: Encloses minutes on Indian, Australian, and New Zealand quotas.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of silk quota minutes to Hartman
subfiles.about: Whitman sends the September 23 silk quota meeting memorandum.
subfiles.summary: Encloses minutes on Indian, Australian, and New Zealand quotas.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of silk quota minutes to Habert
subfiles.about: Whitman sends the September 23 silk quota meeting memorandum.
subfiles.summary: Encloses minutes on Indian, Australian, and New Zealand quotas.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of silk quota minutes to Powles
subfiles.about: Whitman sends the September 23 silk quota meeting memorandum.
subfiles.summary: Encloses minutes on Indian, Australian, and New Zealand quotas.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of silk quota minutes to Trout
subfiles.about: Whitman sends the September 23 silk quota meeting memorandum.
subfiles.summary: Encloses minutes on Indian, Australian, and New Zealand quotas.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of silk quota minutes to Bullock
subfiles.about: Whitman sends the September 23 silk quota meeting memorandum.
subfiles.summary: Encloses minutes on Indian, Australian, and New Zealand quotas.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of silk quota minutes to Banerji
subfiles.about: Whitman sends the September 23 silk quota meeting memorandum.
subfiles.summary: Encloses minutes on Indian, Australian, and New Zealand quotas.

subfiles.title: Enclosure charge slip
subfiles.about: A records charge slip tracks an enclosure.
subfiles.summary: Blank or largely illegible enclosure charge slip.

subfiles.title: British proposal for high grade silk shipments
subfiles.about: Britain requests specific grades, deniers, monthly shipments, and payment terms for Japanese silk.
subfiles.summary: Smart argues that British hosiery needs justify a larger share of fine, high grade silk. He specifies quantities and a five month shipping schedule, with grading after arrival by G. H. Heath & Co. and prices tied to U.S. market averages.

subfiles.title: U.S. reply to British silk proposal
subfiles.about: Whitman addresses British shipment requests, payment, and competing claims to high grade silk.
subfiles.summary: Whitman says SCAP has been advised of the first four requested shipments and finds the proposed sale terms acceptable. He rejects Britain's claim to a larger proportion of scarce fine silk and favors existing percentage quotas as the equitable guide.

subfiles.title: Correction to quota silk price formula
subfiles.about: Whitman clarifies that open auction prices also require averaging for foreign quota purchasers.
subfiles.summary: Prices should average U.S. sales of the same grade and type under either auction method.

subfiles.title: British clarification of sterling payment
subfiles.about: Smart corrects Whitman's understanding of British payment arrangements.
subfiles.summary: Britain proposes sterling payment, with unused sterling convertible into dollars at six month intervals.

subfiles.title: Reply clarifying British payment option
subfiles.about: Whitman clarifies wording in his October 16 letter about Britain's payment option.
subfiles.summary: Whitman says the payment sentence should include the words “at its option.”

subfiles.title: Transmittal of silk quota table to Menon
subfiles.about: Whitman supplies the table distributed at the September 23 quota meeting.
subfiles.summary: Encloses the U.S. Commercial Company silk quota table.

subfiles.title: Pricing Silk Sold
subfiles.about: Whitman seeks SCAP's sale terms and progress in selling silk outside the United States.
subfiles.summary: Draft telegram requests British and Australian sale terms, payment status, and demand forecasts.

subfiles.title: Shipment of Silk to British
subfiles.about: A memorandum recommends approving British shipments and suspending quota limits.
subfiles.summary: Summarizes a proposed cable approving British sales, suspending quotas, and considering future New York auctions.

subfiles.title: Draft reply to SCAP on British shipments and silk pricing
subfiles.about: The draft approves British shipments and sets out temporary quota and pricing policy.
subfiles.summary: The draft approves immediate British shipments, recommends suspending quotas while U.S. processing capacity is limited, and permits government buyers to obtain their requirements. It proposes future New York auctions and discusses how freight, insurance, grading, and other costs should affect prices at a Japanese port.

subfiles.title: British objection to proposed silk valuation
subfiles.about: Britain rejects pricing silk at its value when shipped from Japan.
subfiles.summary: McDougall maintains that an earlier agreement tied payment to U.S. prices after inspection and availability to British buyers. The Board of Trade says shipment date pricing would disadvantage British consumers and questions the reliability of Japanese grading. It also rejects a proposed compromise using an assumed January arrival date.

subfiles.title: State Department advice on British pricing dispute
subfiles.about: Martin recommends negotiations with Britain to resolve disputed sale terms.
subfiles.summary: Martin says State Department discussions did not themselves bind SCAP to a sales contract. He advises SCAP to negotiate complete terms with British representatives and, for silk already shipped, to accept Britain's terms unless another agreement can be established or negotiated.

subfiles.title: Update on 1947 silk sales outside the United States
subfiles.about: Martin relays SCAP estimates of foreign silk demand and pending negotiations.
subfiles.summary: Reports monthly requirements for Australia, New Zealand, Britain, and India and talks with Switzerland and France.

subfiles.title: Withdrawal of New York auction proposal
subfiles.about: The United States withdraws its proposal for exclusive New York raw silk auctions.
subfiles.summary: SCAP and other governments opposed the proposed exclusive U.S. Commercial Company auctions.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of British silk pricing complaint
subfiles.about: Martin acknowledges Britain's complaint and says sale terms must be agreed with SCAP in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Martin describes a misunderstanding and promises further advice on resolving it.

subfiles.title: British account of silk pricing agreement
subfiles.about: McDougall reconstructs the alleged agreement on inspection and pricing of Japanese silk sold to Britain.
subfiles.summary: McDougall says Whitman accepted British inspection by G. H. Heath & Co. and pricing against U.S. market values after inspection. He denies that Britain had been told SCAP would renegotiate those terms. The Board of Trade proposes using current U.S. auction upset prices for silk already shipped, with adjustments for certain grades and Japanese certification.

subfiles.title: Reply to British account of silk pricing
subfiles.about: Martin acknowledges Britain's position and anticipates discussions to resolve the disagreement.
subfiles.summary: Expresses regret for the misunderstanding and hopes for a quick agreement.

subfiles.title: Letter on improving silk textile demand
subfiles.about: Zelomek reports stronger U.S. silk demand and discusses Japanese supply and prices.
subfiles.summary: He reports renewed silk textile production, high finished goods prices, and a rumor that raw silk prices might rise.

subfiles.title: Reply with 1948 silk supply figures
subfiles.about: Whitman provides estimated stocks, production, and sales figures and asks about future demand.
subfiles.summary: Whitman estimates combined U.S. and Japanese stocks at 145,000 bales on May 1 after production and sales. He notes stronger raw silk and fabric sales, possible SCAP interest in expanding sericulture, and uncertainty about price policy. He asks Zelomek for consumption forecasts and whether demand is durable.

subfiles.title: Zelomek reply arranging silk discussion
subfiles.about: Zelomek thanks Whitman for the figures and proposes a Washington discussion.
subfiles.summary: Zelomek plans to call Whitman during his June visit.

subfiles.title: Paterson complaint about Japanese silk fabric imports
subfiles.about: Paterson's Industrial Commission asks the Secretary of State to halt Japanese woven silk imports.
subfiles.summary: Roemer says Japanese fabrics undercut locally woven cloth even after duty and reduce work for Paterson weavers and finishers. He cites 5.594 million yards contracted for U.S. delivery and urges intervention to protect the city's revived silk industry.

subfiles.title: Use of Silk by Distributors Follows an Upward Trend
subfiles.about: A trade article reports rising U.S. purchases of Japanese silk fabrics and increased raw silk consumption.
subfiles.summary: Reports 5.594 million yards contracted from May through August and stronger August raw silk consumption.

subfiles.title: Routing memorandum on reply to Roemer
subfiles.about: An internal note discusses whether to revise a reply after learning Roemer also wrote to MacArthur.
subfiles.summary: Notes MacArthur's request for pricing data and discusses the pending reply.

subfiles.title: Draft reply to Roemer on Japanese silk fabric imports
subfiles.about: State distinguishes predatory dumping from ordinary price competition and explains Japan's need for dollar exports.
subfiles.summary: The draft offers an investigation if Roemer means dumping in its technical sense. It says a natural Japanese price advantage would not establish discrimination and notes that dollar earnings reduce Japan's dependence on U.S. support.

subfiles.title: Reply to Roemer on Japanese silk fabric imports, second copy
subfiles.about: A second copy begins the State Department's response to Roemer's complaint.
subfiles.summary: Repeats the distinction between technical dumping and ordinary price competition; the letter continues beyond this section.
